newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian housing poised to strengthen in 97.
newsitem.headline: Australian housing poised to strengthen in 97.

text.p: Australia's housing sector is poised for recovery in 1997, with emerging growth in the key area of new housing seen as a positive for growth in the economy through the coming year.

The signs of life in the housing sector added to the growing case against the need for a fourth rate cut, although analysts said on Tuesday a cut is not out of the question if, for example, economic data showed renewed weakness.
"The rise in housing finance confirms the buoyant picture for the housing sector in the lead into 1997," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary.
Housing finance approvals rose 5.3 percent in December to be 7.4 percent higher over 1996, official figures on Tuesday showed.

The value of seasonally adjusted housing finance approvals of A$4.219 billion was the fifth highest on record, the four higher readings occuring in between February and May 1994, Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed.
For analysts the most welcome news in the data in recent months has been a rise in finance for construction and new dwellings.
"Approvals for new housing have clearly moved to a higher plateau in the past three months," Bankers Trust Australia chief economist Chris Caton said.

In the December quarter, the monthly average of finance commitments for construction and the purchase of new dwellings was 7,437, up from a monthly averages of 6,729 and 6,622 in the September and June quarters respectively.
Also reflecting the recovery in new housing, refinancing as a percentage of total loans has fallen noticeably in recent months.

After accounting for over 21 percent of total finance approvals each month since October 1995, and peaking at 28.4 percent of approvals in September 1996, refinancing fell to 20 percent of total loans in November, and only rose slightly to 20.9 percent in December.
The fall in interest rates over the second half of 1996 has helped the recovery in housing and economists said the impact of rate cuts in November and December had not yet been seen.
"The improvements in affordability since mid-1996 have been increasingly reflected in a pick up in underlying demand for housing finance," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.
The signs of strength in turn backed up expectations that the economy would strengthen through 1997, with the housing sector seen as helping growth after being a brake on it in recent years.
"Housing is expected to be one of the pillars supporting the economy in 1997," Blythe said.
Growth in new housing could be expected to have flow through effects to employment, manufacturing associated with building materials and sales of household goods, analysts said.
While the signs of a pick up in the housing sector, and the economy more generally, dampened arguments in favour of a fourth rate cut, it did not rule another reduction out.

"We continue to believe that there will believe enough signs of burgeoning growth in the economy that the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia) may never pull the pin on the fourth rate cut," Bankers Trust's Caton said.
"This is a close call however, and we reserve the right to change our mind if, for example, Thursday's (January) labour force report is significantly weaker than expected," he said.
